en: Thus have I heard: the Cūḷasakuludāyisutta, the seventy-ninth discourse in the Majjhima Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time the wanderer Sakuludāyin was residing at the Peacock Sanctuary in the Wanderers’ Park together with a large assembly of wanderers.
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagaha for alms.
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
“It is still too early to wander for alms in Rājagaha.
What if I were to go to the Paribbājaka Arama at Moranivāpa, where the wanderer Sakuludāyī is staying?”
Then the Blessed One approached the wanderers’ park at Moranivāpa.

Now on that occasion the wanderer Sakuludāyin was seated together with a large assembly of wanderers who were making a great clamor and a loud noise, engaged in various kinds of low conversation, such as:
Talk of kings, talk of thieves, talk of ministers, talk of armies, talk of dangers, talk of war, talk of food, talk of drinks, talk of clothing, talk of beds,
talk of garlands, talk of perfumes, talk of relatives, talk of vehicles, talk of villages,
talk of towns, talk of cities, talk of districts, talk of women, talk of heroes, and talk of streets.
“Talk about pots, talk about the departed, talk on diversity, talk about the origin of the world, talk about the origin of the ocean, or talk about ‘thus it was’ and ‘thus it will be.
Then the wanderer Sakuludāyin saw the Blessed One coming from afar.
Seeing him, he quieted his own assembly, saying:
“Be quiet, sirs; do not make a noise.
This ascetic Gotama is approaching;
that venerable one is fond of quietude and speaks in praise of quietude.”
“Perhaps, having perceived that the assembly is quiet, he might think it fit to approach.
Then those wanderers became silent.
Thereupon, the Blessed One approached the wanderer Sakuludāyin.
Then the wanderer Sakuludāyin said this to the Blessed One:
“Come, venerable sir, welcome to the Blessed One.”
"It has been long indeed, Bhante, since the Blessed One made this occasion for coming here.
Let the Blessed One sit down;
this seat is prepared."
The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat.
The wanderer Sakuludāyin also took a certain low seat and sat down to one side.
As the wanderer Sakuludāyin was sitting there to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Udāyī, for what discussion are you sitting gathered here now, and what was your interrupted conversation?
“Let be, Bhante, that discussion for which we are sitting gathered here now.
That discussion, Bhante, will not be difficult for the Blessed One to hear even later on.”
Venerable sir, when I have not yet approached this assembly, this assembly sits engaged in various kinds of worldly talk.
But as soon as I have approached this assembly, venerable sir, this assembly sits looking only toward my face, thinking:
‘We shall hear whatever Dhamma the ascetic Udāyī speaks.’
“But when, venerable sir, the Blessed One has approached this assembly, then both I and this assembly sit looking up at the face of the Blessed One, thinking:
‘We shall hear whatever Dhamma the Blessed One speaks to us.
“In that case, Udāyin, let it be just as it occurs to you here; let me speak according to what occurs to me.”
“Venerable sir, in former days, even earlier than that, there was one who claimed to be all-knowing and all-seeing, to possess knowledge and vision without remainder, saying:
‘Whether I am walking or standing, asleep or awake, knowledge and vision are constantly and continuously present to me.
When questioned by me regarding the past, he prevaricated with irrelevant answers, diverted the conversation to external matters, and manifested anger, hatred, and resentment.”
“Then, venerable sir, mindfulness arose in me concerning the Blessed One himself:
‘Oh, how wonderful it would be if the Blessed One were truly the one most skilled in these teachings!
“But who, Udāyin, is that all-knowing, all-seeing one who claims complete knowledge and vision, [saying]: ‘Whether walking...’?”
‘Whether I am standing, sleeping, or awake, knowledge and vision are constantly and continuously established before me’—
why was it that when you were asked a question concerning the past, you evaded one question with another, diverted the conversation to external matters,
and displayed anger, hatred, and resentment?”
“The Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, Bhante.

“Udāyi, whoever should recollect his manifold past abodes—in this way: one birth, two births …pe… thus with their aspects and particulars he should recollect his manifold past abodes—it is he, or someone like him, who might say to me:”
If one were to ask a question concerning the past, or if I were to ask a question concerning the past;
if he were to satisfy my mind with his answer to that question concerning the past, or if I were to satisfy his mind with my answer to that question concerning the past.
For whoever, Udāyi, with the purified divine eye, surpassing human vision, might see beings passing away...
He would know beings passing away and being reborn—inferior or superior, beautiful or ugly, fortunate or unfortunate—reappearing according to their kamma.
He might ask me a question concerning the future limit, or I might ask him a question concerning the future limit;
he might satisfy my mind with his answer to that question concerning the future limit, or I might satisfy his mind with my answer to that question concerning the future limit.
Moreover, Udāyi, let alone the past, let alone the future.
I shall teach you the Dhamma:
when this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises.
“When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases.
“Venerable sir, even regarding what has been personally experienced by me throughout this present life, I am unable to recollect it with its modes and particulars;

how then could I recollect my manifold past abodes, such as one birth, two births... [and so on]... thus recollecting my manifold past abodes with their modes and particulars, just as the Blessed One does?”
"Indeed, venerable sir, at present I do not even see a dust-demon;
how then could I, with the divine eye— purified and surpassing that of humans— see beings passing away and being reborn,
inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understand how beings fare according to their kamma, as the Blessed One does?"
But as for what the Blessed One said to me, venerable sir:
“Moreover, Udāyin, let alone the past, let alone the future;
I will teach you the Dhamma.”
‘When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises.
When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases. Yet even so, I am not fully satisfied by this answer.
Perhaps, venerable sir, I might satisfy the Blessed One’s mind regarding this question by means of my own teacher’s doctrine.”
“But how, Udāyin, is it in your own teacher’s tradition?
“In our own teacher’s tradition, Bhante, it is thus:
‘This is the supreme beauty; this is the supreme beauty.’”
“But, Udāyin, as for this which you hold in your own teacher’s tradition:
‘This is the supreme beauty; this is the supreme beauty’—what is that supreme beauty?
“Venerable sir, that beauty beyond which there is no other beauty higher or more sublime—that is the supreme beauty.”
“But what, Udāyī, is that supreme beauty, beyond which there is no other beauty higher or more sublime?
“That beauty, venerable sir, beyond which there is no other beauty higher or more sublime—that is the supreme beauty.
“Indeed, Udāyī, you could go on at length:”
“Venerable sir, you say: ‘That beauty beyond which there is no other beauty higher or more sublime—that is the supreme beauty,’ yet you do not define what that beauty is.
It is just as if, Udāyin, a man were to say:
‘I desire and love the most beautiful woman in this country.’”
They would say to him:
“Good man, do you know whether that most beautiful woman in the land whom you desire and lust after is a kṣatriyan woman, or a brahmin woman, or a vaiśya woman, or a śūdra woman?
Being asked this, he would say: “No.”
They would say this to him:
"O man, regarding that most beautiful woman in the land whom you desire and lust after, do you know that most beautiful woman in the land—her name and her clan? ...
[and so on] ... whether she is tall, short, or of medium height; whether she is dark, fair, or of golden complexion?"
“Does it blow in such-and-such a village, town, or city?
Being asked thus, he would say, “No.
Then they would say to him:
“‘O man, do you desire and long for that which you neither know nor see?
Being asked thus, he would say, ‘Yes.
What do you think, Udāyin?”
“But if that were so, would not the speech of that man turn out to be unconvincing?
“Certainly, venerable sir, if that were so, the speech of that man would turn out to be unconvincing.
“In the same way, Udāyin, you say, ‘Venerable sir, there is no other beauty higher or more sublime than this beauty; that is the supreme beauty,’ yet you do not define what that beauty is.”

“Venerable sir, just as a beautiful beryl gem of pure birth, cut with eight facets and well-polished, lying on a white woolen cloth, gleams, glows, and radiates—of such a color is the self, healthy after death.
“What do you think, Udāyin?
As for that beautiful beryl gem of pure birth, cut with eight facets and well-polished, lying on a white woolen cloth...”
"It shines, it glows, and it radiates; or else there is the glowworm in the thick darkness of the night.
Of these two colors, which color is more excellent and more sublime?
"Venerable sir, that glowworm in the thick darkness of the night—this color is more excellent and more sublime than these two."
“What do you think, Udāyin?
Between a glowworm in the thick darkness of the night and an oil lamp in the thick darkness of the night—which of these two things has the more excellent and sublime appearance?
“Venerable sir, the oil lamp in the thick darkness of the night has the more excellent and sublime appearance of these two things.”
“What do you think, Udāyin?
Between a lamp fed with oil in the thick darkness of the night and a great mass of fire in the thick darkness of the night—which of these two appearances is more excellent and sublime?
“Venerable sir, that which is a great mass of fire in the thick darkness of the night is more excellent and sublime than these two appearances.”
“What do you think, Udāyin?
Between a great mass of fire in the pitch-black darkness of night and the star Osadhī at the time of dawn on a clear,
cloudless night— which of these two appearances is more excellent?”
"And which is more excellent and sublime?
"Venerable sir, that star Osadhi when it is dawn, the sky being clear and cloudless—this is more excellent and sublime than both of those colors.
"What do you think, Udāyi?"
“Or like the morning star at the time of dawn on a clear night when the clouds have dispersed,
or like the moon at midnight on the fifteenth day of the uposatha, a clear night when the clouds have dispersed—
which of these two colors is more excellent and more sublime?”
“Venerable sir, on the Uposatha day of the fifteenth, when the sky is clear and free of clouds, the moon at midnight—this is more excellent and more sublime than the beauty of these two.
“What do you think, Udāyī?
Between the moon on that Uposatha day of the fifteenth, when the sky is clear and free of clouds at midnight...”
“The moon, or the sun at midday in the last month of the rainy season during the autumn time when the sky is clear and free of clouds—
which of these two colors is more excellent and more sublime?

“Venerable sir, that which is the sun at midday in the last month of the rainy season during the autumn time when the sky is clear and free of clouds— that is the more excellent and more sublime of these two colors.”
“Thus, Udāyin, there are indeed many more gods than those who do not experience the radiance of these suns and moons; these I know.
And yet, I do not say:
‘There is no other beauty higher or more sublime than this beauty.’”
“Yet, Udāyī, you say: ‘That color which is inferior and more loathsome than that of a glowworm is the supreme color,’ and yet you do not define what that color is.
“Bhagavā, you have cut through my doubt; Sugata, you have cut through my doubt.
“But why, Udāyī, do you speak thus?”
“Has the Blessed One answered clearly, has the Sugata answered clearly?
“Venerable sir, in our own teacher’s tradition it is said:
‘This is the supreme excellence; this is the supreme excellence.’”
“Thus, venerable sir, when we were questioned, cross-examined, and interrogated by the Blessed One regarding our own teacher’s doctrine, we were found empty, hollow, and lacking.
“But what, Udāyin, is this ‘entirely happy world,’ and is there a methodical practice for the realization of that entirely happy world?
“Venerable sir, it is our view in our own teacher’s doctrine that:”
“There is a world of absolute happiness; there is a methodical practice for the realization of that world of absolute happiness.
“But what, Udāyin, is that methodical practice for the realization of that world of absolute happiness?
“Here, venerable sir, someone, having abandoned the taking of life, abstains from taking life; having abandoned the taking of what is not given...”
Having abandoned taking what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given; having abandoned sexual misconduct, he abstains from sexual misconduct;
having abandoned false speech, he abstains from false speech; or else, having undertaken some quality of asceticism, he practices it.
This, venerable sir, is that methodical practice for the realization of an exclusively happy world.”
“What do you think, Udāyin,
at the time when one has abandoned the taking of life and abstains from taking life, is the self at that time exclusively happy, or is it both happy and suffering?
“Both happy and suffering, Bhante.”
“What do you think, Udāyin,
at the time when one has abandoned taking what is not given and abstains from taking what is not given, is the self at that time exclusively happy, or is it both happy and suffering?
“Both happy and suffering, Bhante.”
“What do you think, Udāyin, at the time when one has abandoned sexual misconduct and abstains from sexual misconduct, is the self at that time exclusively happy, or is it both happy and suffering?
“Both happy and suffering, Bhante.
“What do you think, Udāyin, at the time when one has abandoned false speech and abstains from false speech, is the self at that time exclusively happy, or is it both happy and suffering?”
“Experiencing both pleasure and pain, venerable sir.
“What do you think, Udāyin?
At the time when one practices having undertaken some quality of asceticism, is the self at that time exclusively happy, or is it experiencing both pleasure and pain?”
“Experiencing both pleasure and pain, venerable sir.
“What do you think, Udāyin?
Could the realization of an exclusively happy world come about by means of a practice that is mixed with pleasure and pain?”
“The Blessed One has cut off talk, the Sublime One has cut off talk.
“But what, Udāyī, are you saying when you say:
‘The Blessed One has cut off talk, the Sublime One has cut off talk’?”
“Venerable sir, it is our own teachers’ doctrine that:
‘There is an exclusively happy world; there is a methodical practice for the realization of an exclusively happy world.
But when we were questioned, pressed, and cross-examined by the Blessed One regarding our own teachers’ doctrine, we were found empty, hollow, and at fault.”
“But, venerable sir, is there a world of absolute happiness? Is there a methodical practice for the realization of a world of absolute happiness?
“There is, Udāyin, a world of absolute happiness; there is a methodical practice for the realization of a world of absolute happiness.
“But what, venerable sir, is that methodical practice for the realization of a world of absolute happiness?”
“Here, Udāyi, secluded from sensual pleasures, a bhikkhu … enters and dwells in the first jhāna;
with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought … he enters and dwells in the second jhāna;
and with the fading away of rapture … he enters and dwells in the third jhāna.
“Indeed, Udāyi, this is that methodical practice for the realization of an entirely happy world.
“But, Bhante, that is not a methodical practice for the realization of an entirely happy world; for, Bhante, at this point the entirely happy world has already been realized by him.
“Udāyi, it is not at this point that the entirely happy world has been realized by him;”
"But that path is indeed possessed of form for the realization of an exclusively happy world.
When this was said, the assembly of the wanderer Sakuludāyin broke into loud noise and great clamor:
"We have been lost here along with our teacher! We have been lost here along with our teacher!"
“We do not know anything superior to this.
Then the wanderer Sakuludāyin, having silenced those wanderers, addressed the Blessed One:
“But to what extent, venerable sir, has the world of absolute happiness been realized?”
“Here, Udāyi, with the abandoning of pleasure... [as above] ...a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
He stands, converses, and engages in discussion with those deities who have been reborn in a world of exclusive happiness.
To this extent, Udāyi, a world of exclusive happiness has been realized by him.”
“Venerable sir, is it not for the sake of realizing this world of absolute happiness that bhikkhus lead the holy life under the Blessed One?
“Udāyi, it is not for the sake of realizing a world of absolute happiness that bhikkhus lead the holy life under me.
There are, Udāyi, other states even more supreme and more sublime than that, for the sake of realizing which bhikkhus lead the holy life under me.”
“But what, venerable sir, are those things that are higher and more sublime, for the sake of realizing which bhikkhus lead the holy life under the Blessed One?

“In this case, Udāyi, a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Well-Gone One, a knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One...
Having abandoned these five hindrances—defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom...”
“Quite secluded from sensual pleasures... [he] enters and dwells in the first jhāna.
This, Udāyi, is a Dhamma that is higher and more sublime, for the sake of realizing which bhikkhus lead the holy life under me.
Furthermore, Udāyi, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought... [he] enters and dwells in the second jhāna.”
He enters and dwells in the third jhāna… and the fourth jhāna.
This too, Udāyi, is a Dhamma that is higher and more sublime, for the sake of realizing which bhikkhus lead the holy life under me.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it toward the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
He recollects his manifold past lives, that is to say: one birth, two births... [as far as] thus with their aspects and particulars he recollects his manifold past lives.
"Udāyi, this too is a Dhamma that is higher and more sublime than that, for the sake of realizing which bhikkhus lead the holy life under me.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it toward the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings."

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma.
This, Udāyi, is a Dhamma that is higher and more sublime than the former, for the sake of realizing which bhikkhus lead the holy life under me.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it toward the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.

He understands as it really is: “This is suffering”; ... “This is the origin of suffering” ... “This is the cessation of suffering” ... “This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering,” as it really is.

He understands as it really is: "These are the taints"; he understands as it really is: "This is the origin of the taints"; he understands as it really is: "This is the cessation of the taints"; he understands as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of the taints.
For one who knows and sees thus, the mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, the mind is liberated from the taint of existence, and the mind is liberated from the taint of ignorance.
When liberated, the knowledge arises: "It is liberated."
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being’—he understands this.
This too, Udāyi, is a Dhamma that is higher and more sublime than the former, for the sake of realizing which bhikkhus live the holy life under me.
These, Udāyi, are the dharmas that are higher and more sublime than those, for the sake of realizing which bhikkhus live the holy life under me.”
When this was said, the wanderer Sakuludāyin said to the Blessed One:
“Excellent, Bhante! Excellent, Bhante!
Just as, Bhante, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost...”
Or as one might show the way to one who is lost, or as one might hold up an oil lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—
just so has the Dhamma been proclaimed by the Blessed One in many ways.
Therefore, venerable sir, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
“Venerable sir, may I receive the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; may I receive full ordination.
When this was said, the assembly of the wanderer Sakuludāyin said this to the wanderer Sakuludāyin:
“Do not, Master Udāyin, lead the holy life under the ascetic Gotama.”
"Venerable Udāyin, do not live as a pupil while being a teacher.
It would be just as if one were a water-jar yet became a water-dipper; such will be the situation for the venerable Udāyin.
Do not, venerable Udāyin, lead the holy life under the ascetic Gotama."
“Venerable Udāyin, do not live as a pupil under a teacher.
Thus, this assembly of the wanderer Sakuludāyin created an obstacle for the wanderer Sakuludāyin regarding the holy life under the Blessed One.
The Cūḷasakuludāyisutta, the ninth, is finished.
